items.prompt: In this unit's terms, what is "config"?
choices: Anything that legitimately varies by environment without the code itself changing (a timeout, a DB URL, a feature flag)
Any comment left in the source code explaining a decision
The version-control history of a repository
A synonym for the deployed container image itself
items.explanation: Config is the set of values that should differ by environment while the code stays identical — that separation is what lets one built artifact run correctly everywhere.
items.reference:
🧱 code = logic that behaves identically everywhere
🎛️ config = values that legitimately vary by environment

Why: Keeping the two separate is what lets one build run correctly in every environment.

items.prompt: Why is a payment timeout value considered config rather than code, in this unit's framing?
choices: Because it's a value that legitimately differs by environment (staging's low latency vs. production's real load), not logic that should behave the same everywhere
Because timeouts are always stored in a database table
Because it's measured in milliseconds instead of seconds
Because only senior engineers are allowed to change it
items.explanation: A timeout tuned for one environment's real conditions is exactly the kind of value that's supposed to differ per environment — that's what makes it config, not code.
items.reference:
🧱 code = logic that behaves identically everywhere
🎛️ config = values that legitimately vary by environment

Why: Keeping the two separate is what lets one build run correctly in every environment.

items.prompt: L1's Scenario says the payment code was "identical" between staging and production. What does that tell you about where the bug lived?
choices: The bug lived in a config value (an unset environment variable), not in the application logic itself
It tells you the bug must have been in the test suite instead
It proves there was no real bug, just user error
It means the bug was actually a network outage unrelated to config
items.explanation: Identical code with different behavior points directly at something outside the code — in this case, a config value that was set in staging and silently defaulted in production.
items.reference:
🧱 code = logic that behaves identically everywhere
🎛️ config = values that legitimately vary by environment

Why: Keeping the two separate is what lets one build run correctly in every environment.

items.prompt: What actually caused L1's production checkout failures?
choices: PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_MS was never set in production, so the code silently fell back to a 3-second default that was too short for production's real latency
A new deploy shipped broken payment logic that staging's tests didn't cover
Production's payment provider was down for the entire incident
Staging and production were running two different versions of the container image
items.explanation: The container image was identical in both environments — the only difference was a missing environment variable in production, which triggered a silent 3-second default instead of the tested 30-second value.
items.reference:
🧪 staging: timeout set to 30000ms explicitly
☁️ production: unset, silently defaulted to 3000ms

Why: A silent default made a missing value indistinguishable from a deliberate one.

items.prompt: Why did staging's tests never catch the timeout problem before it reached production?
choices: Staging had the environment variable set correctly, so it never exercised the silent-default fallback path at all
Staging doesn't run any automated tests
The payment provider only exists in production, not in staging
Staging's tests were skipped for that release
items.explanation: Staging's explicit 30-second setting meant its tests always ran against the intended value — the fallback path only ever executed in production, where the variable was missing.
items.reference:
🧪 staging: timeout set to 30000ms explicitly
☁️ production: unset, silently defaulted to 3000ms

Why: A silent default made a missing value indistinguishable from a deliberate one.

items.prompt: Why was the deploy itself not a useful signal that something was wrong in L1's scenario?
choices: The deploy succeeded normally — the service started, passed its health check, and served most traffic fine; only requests hitting the slow payment path failed
The deploy actually failed outright and was rolled back automatically
The deploy took an unusually long time to complete
The deploy pipeline reported a config error that was ignored
items.explanation: Nothing about the deploy or the service's startup looked wrong — the service ran, accepted connections, and served most requests; only checkouts hitting the slow real-latency path revealed the missing value.
items.reference:
🧪 staging: timeout set to 30000ms explicitly
☁️ production: unset, silently defaulted to 3000ms

Why: A silent default made a missing value indistinguishable from a deliberate one.

items.prompt: What is an environment variable, in the config-management sense used here?
choices: A named value set outside the application's source code, read by the running process at startup or during a request
A variable declared with `let` instead of `const` in JavaScript
A column in a production database table
A comment describing what an environment is used for
items.explanation: An environment variable is a value supplied to the running process from outside the code — simple to use, but with nothing enforcing that it's actually set until the code tries to read it.
items.reference:
➕ simple, no extra tooling
⚠️ easy to typo or forget to set

Why: Nothing enforces an env var exists until the code that reads it actually runs.

items.prompt: What is the main downside of relying on environment variables for required config?
choices: There's nothing that automatically stops you from forgetting to set one in a given environment — the omission is silent unless something explicitly checks for it
Environment variables can only hold numbers, never strings
They can never be changed without editing the application's source code
They are automatically shared across every environment, so they can't differ at all
items.explanation: A forgotten environment variable produces no error by itself — that silence is exactly what let L1's missing timeout variable go unnoticed until real traffic hit it.
items.reference:
➕ simple, no extra tooling
⚠️ easy to typo or forget to set

Why: Nothing enforces an env var exists until the code that reads it actually runs.

items.prompt: What is a secrets manager used for in config management?
choices: Storing sensitive config values (API keys, database credentials) with encryption and audit access, instead of plain environment variables or files
Generating random test data for staging
Compressing config files to save disk space
Replacing version control for application source code
items.explanation: A secrets manager is specifically for the sensitive subset of config — credentials and keys — that shouldn't sit in plain environment variables or be committed to a config file in version control.
items.reference:
🔐 encrypted, audited, rotatable
⚠️ adds a real runtime dependency

Why: Real security for sensitive values, at the cost of real operational complexity.

items.prompt: What is a real cost of using a secrets manager, versus a plain environment variable?
choices: It adds a runtime dependency — the service can't start correctly if it can't reach the secrets manager
It makes secrets visible in the source code repository
It prevents the value from ever being rotated or changed
It's slower to read than a database query on every single request
items.explanation: Reaching out to a secrets manager at startup (or on each fetch) introduces a new dependency the service now relies on being available — real security, but real added operational surface.
items.reference:
🔐 encrypted, audited, rotatable
⚠️ adds a real runtime dependency

Why: Real security for sensitive values, at the cost of real operational complexity.

items.prompt: What does "fail fast" mean in the context of config?
choices: Checking required config is present and well-formed at startup, and refusing to start if it isn't, rather than discovering the problem mid-request
Making the service respond to requests as quickly as possible
Automatically retrying a failed request several times before giving up
Deleting a config file as soon as it's no longer needed
items.explanation: Fail-fast config validation means checking everything required is present and valid before the service accepts any traffic, so a bad config produces an immediate, loud startup failure instead of a silent, delayed one.
items.reference:
🚨 checked at startup = loud, immediate
🤫 found mid-request = quiet, delayed

Why: A service that never starts is obviously broken; a service that starts broken looks healthy until real traffic finds the gap.

items.prompt: If L1's production service had used fail-fast config validation, what would have happened differently?
choices: The service would have refused to start and printed a clear error about the missing timeout variable, before ever serving a checkout request
The service would have started normally, exactly as it did
The payment provider itself would have been automatically fixed
Staging's tests would have caught the bug instead
items.explanation: Fail-fast validation moves the discovery of a missing required value from "a customer's failed checkout" to "the deploy process, before traffic is served" — same bug, much earlier and much louder.
items.reference:
🚨 checked at startup = loud, immediate
🤫 found mid-request = quiet, delayed

Why: A service that never starts is obviously broken; a service that starts broken looks healthy until real traffic finds the gap.

items.prompt: Why is "the service started and passed its health check" not the same claim as "the service is correctly configured"?
choices: A typical health check only confirms the process is up and responsive — it doesn't inspect whether every required config value is present and reasonable
Health checks always run config validation as part of their logic
Health checks are only used in staging, never in production
A service can't pass a health check unless its config is already fully valid
items.explanation: A shallow health check pings that the process is alive; it doesn't exercise the specific code paths that depend on a given config value, which is exactly why L1's service looked healthy while quietly broken.
items.reference:
🚨 checked at startup = loud, immediate
🤫 found mid-request = quiet, delayed

Why: A service that never starts is obviously broken; a service that starts broken looks healthy until real traffic finds the gap.

items.prompt: What does "build once, configure per environment" mean?
choices: The same built artifact (e.g. container image) is promoted unchanged through every environment, with only externally-supplied config differing between them
Each environment gets its own separately built version of the application
Config values are baked into the container image at build time, one image per environment
The application is rebuilt every time a config value changes
items.explanation: Building once means the artifact tested in staging is byte-for-byte the artifact running in production — only externally-injected config differs, never the code itself.
items.reference:
🏗️ build once = one artifact, no environment baked in
🎛️ configure per environment = values injected at deploy time

Why: The thing you tested is the exact thing you ship — nothing rebuilt, nothing re-resolved per stage.

items.prompt: Why would baking a database URL directly into a container image at build time defeat the point of "build once"?
choices: It would either point every environment at the same database, or force a separate rebuild per environment — undermining the promise that the exact tested artifact is what ships
It would make the image build noticeably faster
It would make config validation unnecessary
Container images cannot technically contain environment variables at all
items.explanation: Baking an environment-specific value into the artifact itself reintroduces the need to rebuild per environment, or produces the wrong value everywhere it's not meant for — either way, it breaks the single-artifact model.
items.reference:
🏗️ build once = one artifact, no environment baked in
🎛️ configure per environment = values injected at deploy time

Why: The thing you tested is the exact thing you ship — nothing rebuilt, nothing re-resolved per stage.

items.prompt: How does this unit's "build once, configure per environment" idea relate to `deployment-automation`'s pipeline model?
choices: `deployment-automation` covers promoting the same artifact through a pipeline without rebuilding it; this unit covers what makes that promotion safe — keeping environment-specific values out of the artifact entirely
They are unrelated concepts that happen to share vocabulary
`deployment-automation` is only about config, this unit is only about code
This unit replaces the need for a deploy pipeline entirely
items.explanation: The two connect directly: a pipeline that promotes one artifact through stages only works cleanly if that artifact has no environment-specific values baked in — which is precisely this unit's config-vs-code separation.
items.reference:
🏗️ build once = one artifact, no environment baked in
🎛️ configure per environment = values injected at deploy time

Why: The thing you tested is the exact thing you ship — nothing rebuilt, nothing re-resolved per stage.

items.prompt: What is the main trade-off of using a per-environment config file instead of environment variables?
choices: It's versioned and reviewable in a pull request, but it can't safely hold secrets like API keys or database passwords
It's faster to read at runtime but can only hold a single value
It requires no tooling at all, unlike environment variables
It automatically encrypts every value it stores
items.explanation: A config file gives you diffable, reviewable history for non-sensitive values, but committing secrets into it puts them in version control history — exactly what a secrets manager exists to avoid.
items.reference:
📄 env vars: simple, easy to forget silently
🗂️ config files: reviewable, can't hold secrets safely
🔐 secrets manager: secure, adds operational complexity

Why: Most real services mix all three by what each value actually needs.

items.prompt: Which of these config values would most sensibly live in a secrets manager rather than a plain config file?
choices: A production database password
A feature flag's default on/off state
The number of retry attempts for an HTTP call
The name of the current deploy environment (e.g. "staging")
items.explanation: A database password is a sensitive credential — exactly the category a secrets manager is designed for. Feature flags, retry counts, and environment names carry no security risk if visible in a config file.
items.reference:
📄 env vars: simple, easy to forget silently
🗂️ config files: reviewable, can't hold secrets safely
🔐 secrets manager: secure, adds operational complexity

Why: Most real services mix all three by what each value actually needs.

items.prompt: Why do most real services use a mix of environment variables, config files, and a secrets manager, rather than just one mechanism for everything?
choices: Because each mechanism has a different real trade-off, and different config values (non-sensitive vs. sensitive, simple vs. structured) fit different mechanisms best
Because using only one mechanism is technically impossible in most deploy systems
Because regulations require using at least three separate config systems
Because a single mechanism would be slower to read at runtime
items.explanation: The mechanisms aren't interchangeable — a secrets manager solves a problem plain env vars can't (safe secrets), while env vars solve a problem a secrets manager overkills (a simple non-sensitive toggle), so real services pick per value.
items.reference:
📄 env vars: simple, easy to forget silently
🗂️ config files: reviewable, can't hold secrets safely
🔐 secrets manager: secure, adds operational complexity

Why: Most real services mix all three by what each value actually needs.

items.prompt: How does config management differ from environment parity, in what each is trying to achieve?
choices: Parity eliminates accidental drift in the environment executing the code (OS, runtime, libraries); config management manages intentional, necessary differences in the values fed into identical code
They are the same goal described with two different names
Parity is only about databases, config management is only about APIs
Config management replaces the need for environment parity entirely
items.explanation: Parity targets the executing environment being identical everywhere; config management targets making sure the values that are supposed to differ, differ correctly and on purpose — different axes, both needed.
items.reference:
🧬 parity: environment should be identical (accidental drift is the enemy)
🎛️ config: values should legitimately differ (silent mistakes are the enemy)

Why: "Different" isn't the problem here — "different by accident" is.

items.prompt: Staging and production intentionally point at different databases. Is that a parity violation?
choices: No — that's expected, legitimate config variation, not the kind of accidental drift parity is concerned with
Yes — parity requires every environment to be byte-for-byte identical in every respect, including data
Yes, but only if the two databases run different software versions
It's undefined — parity and config management don't overlap at all
items.explanation: Parity is about the executing environment (OS, runtime, libraries), not about environment-specific config values like a database connection string, which are expected to differ by design.
items.reference:
🧬 parity: environment should be identical (accidental drift is the enemy)
🎛️ config: values should legitimately differ (silent mistakes are the enemy)

Why: "Different" isn't the problem here — "different by accident" is.

items.prompt: In the build → configure → validate → serve model from L2's diagram, what happens if validation fails?
choices: The service refuses to start and never begins serving traffic, rather than starting in a broken state
The service starts anyway but logs a warning
The build pipeline automatically retries with a different config value
The failure is silently ignored and the previous config is reused
items.explanation: The whole point of putting validation before "serve traffic" in the flow is that a failure there blocks traffic entirely — the service never gets the chance to run in a state where required config is missing or malformed.
items.reference:
🏗️ build → configure → validate → serve
⛔ validation fails → refuse to start, no traffic served

Why: A service that never starts is loud and immediate; a service that starts broken is quiet and delayed.

items.prompt: Why is validating config at startup better than validating it lazily, the first time each value is used?
choices: Lazy validation only catches a problem when the code path that uses that value actually runs, which for a rarely-hit path could be long after deploy, deep inside real traffic
Lazy validation is technically impossible to implement
Startup validation is always faster to execute than lazy validation
There's no real difference between the two approaches
items.explanation: L1's bug is the exact failure mode lazy validation misses — the broken timeout value sat unused until the first slow real request finally exercised that code path, long after the service had already started serving traffic.
items.reference:
🏗️ build → configure → validate → serve
⛔ validation fails → refuse to start, no traffic served

Why: A service that never starts is loud and immediate; a service that starts broken is quiet and delayed.

items.prompt: Where does startup config validation sit relative to the load balancer adding a new instance to rotation?
choices: Before it — a service that fails validation should never be added to rotation to receive real traffic
After it — instances are always added to rotation before their config is checked
The two are unrelated and happen independently
Validation replaces the need for a load balancer entirely
items.explanation: The value of fail-fast validation depends on it happening before the instance can serve any real request — if it ran after rotation, a broken instance could already be handling live traffic by the time it's caught.
items.reference:
🏗️ build → configure → validate → serve
⛔ validation fails → refuse to start, no traffic served

Why: A service that never starts is loud and immediate; a service that starts broken is quiet and delayed.

items.prompt: If a config value needs to change, what should change under the "build once, configure per environment" model?
choices: The externally-supplied config for that environment — not the build artifact itself
The build artifact must always be rebuilt from scratch
The application's source code must be edited directly
Nothing can change once an artifact is built, ever, for any reason
items.explanation: Config lives outside the artifact specifically so it can change independently — updating a config value means updating what's injected at deploy time, not touching or rebuilding the artifact.
items.reference:
📦 artifact: built once, stays fixed
🎛️ config: injected at deploy time, changes independently

Why: That separation is exactly what makes config changes cheap and artifact changes deliberate.

items.prompt: What would be lost if config values were compiled directly into the build artifact instead of injected at deploy time?
choices: The ability to promote the exact same tested artifact through every environment without rebuilding it per environment
The ability to run automated tests on the artifact at all
The ability to use a secrets manager for any value
Nothing would be lost — it would work identically either way
items.explanation: Compiling config into the artifact reintroduces the need for a separate build per environment, which is precisely what "build once, configure per environment" is designed to avoid.
items.reference:
📦 artifact: built once, stays fixed
🎛️ config: injected at deploy time, changes independently

Why: That separation is exactly what makes config changes cheap and artifact changes deliberate.

items.prompt: Complete `validateConfig(config)` so it throws an Error with message "missing required config: paymentApiKey" if `config.paymentApiKey` is missing or empty, and throws "missing required config: paymentTimeoutMs" if `config.paymentTimeoutMs` is missing or not a finite number. Otherwise it returns `config` unchanged.

tests.description: throws when paymentTimeoutMs is not a number

items.explanation: Each required field gets an explicit presence-and-type check that throws a clear, named error the moment it's missing or malformed — this is what turns a silently-missing value into a loud startup failure instead of a runtime surprise.
items.reference:
✅ present + well-formed → return config
❌ missing/malformed → throw a named error immediately

Why: A clear thrown error at startup is the loud version of the same check L1's silent default skipped.

items.prompt: Complete `validateConfig(config)` so it throws an Error with message "missing required config: dbUrl" if `config.dbUrl` is missing or empty, and throws "missing required config: maxConnections" if `config.maxConnections` is missing or not a finite number. Otherwise it returns `config` unchanged.

tests.description: throws when maxConnections is not a number

items.explanation: Same pattern as any required config field: an explicit presence-and-type check per value, throwing a clearly-named error immediately rather than letting a missing value slip through to be discovered later.
items.reference:
✅ present + well-formed → return config
❌ missing/malformed → throw a named error immediately

Why: A clear thrown error at startup is the loud version of the same check L1's silent default skipped.

items.prompt: This function reproduces L1's exact bug: a missing `PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_MS` silently falls back to 3000 instead of failing. Fix `loadPaymentConfig(env)` so it throws an Error if `env.PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_MS` is missing, and otherwise returns `{ timeoutMs: <the numeric value> }`.

tests.description: throws when the env var is missing
returns the parsed numeric value when set
returns a different parsed value correctly

items.explanation: Removing the silent `: 3000` fallback and replacing it with an explicit throw is the entire fix — it converts an unset environment variable from a quietly-accepted default into a loud startup failure, exactly like L1's real incident should have produced.
items.reference:
🚨 before: unset var → silent 3000ms default
✅ after: unset var → thrown startup error

Why: A required value's default should never be indistinguishable from "nobody set it."

items.prompt: This function has the same bug class as L1's scenario, for a feature flag instead of a timeout: a missing `FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT` silently defaults to `false` with no way to tell "deliberately off" from "forgotten." Fix `loadFeatureFlagConfig(env)` so it throws an Error if `env.FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT` is missing entirely, and otherwise returns `{ newCheckoutEnabled: <boolean> }` based on whether the value equals the string "true".

tests.description: throws when the env var is missing entirely
returns true when explicitly set to "true"
returns false when explicitly set to "false"

items.explanation: Checking specifically for `undefined` (not just falsiness) distinguishes "the variable was never set" from "the variable was explicitly set to false" — the same silent-default trap as a numeric timeout, just for a boolean.
items.reference:
🚨 before: unset var → silent 3000ms default
✅ after: unset var → thrown startup error

Why: A required value's default should never be indistinguishable from "nobody set it."

items.prompt: Complete `validateRateLimit(requestsPerSecond)` so it throws an Error if the value is not a positive finite number, or if it exceeds 100000 (a value nobody would sanely configure). Otherwise it returns the value unchanged. This should accept both a small staging value and a much larger production value, since both are legitimate.

tests.description: throws on an absurdly large value

items.explanation: The range is wide enough to accept any legitimate per-environment value (staging's 20 or production's 2000) while still rejecting the shapes of mistake — zero, negative, or absurdly large — that a presence-only check would miss.
items.reference:
✅ staging 20 req/s and prod 2000 req/s both pass
❌ negative, zero, or absurdly large values fail

Why: A range wide enough for legitimate variation, narrow enough to catch an obvious typo.

items.prompt: Complete `validateTimeoutMs(timeoutMs)` so it throws an Error if the value is not a positive finite number, or if it falls outside the sane range of 1000 to 60000 (milliseconds). Otherwise it returns the value unchanged. This should accept both staging's 30000 and a different, still-reasonable production value.

tests.description: accepts a different reasonable production value

items.explanation: This is the same range-check shape as L3's worked example — wide enough to hold any timeout a human would deliberately configure, narrow enough to reject the exact class of typo (a stray missing digit) that presence checks alone can't catch.
items.reference:
✅ staging 20 req/s and prod 2000 req/s both pass
❌ negative, zero, or absurdly large values fail

Why: A range wide enough for legitimate variation, narrow enough to catch an obvious typo.

items.prompt: Staging runs a rate limit of 20 req/s, production runs 2000 req/s. Is this a misconfiguration?
choices: No — this is expected, legitimate variation, since production genuinely serves far more real traffic than staging
Yes — both environments must always use the exact same rate limit
Yes, because a 100x difference always indicates a typo
It can't be determined without seeing the source code
items.explanation: A large numeric gap between environments isn't itself evidence of a mistake — production and staging are sized for very different real loads, so a proportionally large difference in a capacity-related value like a rate limit is exactly what's expected.
items.reference:
✅ staging 20, prod 2000 — both correct, intentional
❌ staging 20, prod 2 (typo) — same shape, but wrong

Why: A validator tight enough to catch the typo would also block the legitimate value — the line has to be a sane-range check, not an exact-match check.

items.prompt: A validator rejects any production rate limit that isn't within 20% of staging's value. What real problem does this cause?
choices: It would block legitimate, correctly-scaled production deploys, since production is supposed to differ from staging by a large margin
It has no downside — it's strictly stricter and therefore strictly safer
It would only ever reject genuine typos and nothing else
It would make the deploy faster by skipping validation entirely
items.explanation: A tight relative-match check conflates "differs from staging" with "wrong" — but production is supposed to differ substantially from staging here, so this check would block the correct, intended value along with genuine mistakes.
items.reference:
✅ staging 20, prod 2000 — both correct, intentional
❌ staging 20, prod 2 (typo) — same shape, but wrong

Why: A validator tight enough to catch the typo would also block the legitimate value — the line has to be a sane-range check, not an exact-match check.

items.prompt: What kind of check successfully tells apart "production's rate limit is legitimately much higher than staging's" from "production's rate limit was accidentally typed with a missing digit"?
choices: A sane outer-bound range check (e.g. positive and under some very high cap) rather than a check comparing production's value against staging's specific value
A check that production's value must always exceed staging's by exactly 100x
There is no check that can ever distinguish these two cases
A check that simply logs a warning but never blocks the deploy either way
items.explanation: An outer-bound range check accepts any value a human might sanely choose for either environment, while still catching the obviously-wrong shapes (zero, negative, or a value with a missing digit) — it doesn't try to guess the "right" number for either environment specifically.
items.reference:
✅ staging 20, prod 2000 — both correct, intentional
❌ staging 20, prod 2 (typo) — same shape, but wrong

Why: A validator tight enough to catch the typo would also block the legitimate value — the line has to be a sane-range check, not an exact-match check.

items.prompt: A rate limit of 2000 req/s passes every presence and range check. Does that guarantee 2000 is the right value for production right now?
choices: No — validation can confirm the value is well-formed and plausible, but whether it's the correct value for current real conditions is a human capacity-planning judgment
Yes — passing validation is equivalent to being operationally correct
Yes, because range checks are specifically designed to know the ideal value per environment
No, because passing validation always means the value is definitely wrong
items.explanation: Validation's job ends at "this value is well-formed and within sane bounds" — whether 2000 is actually the right number for today's traffic (versus, say, an upcoming spike) is a decision a range check has no way to make.
items.reference:
⚙️ validation catches: missing, malformed, absurd
🧠 validation can't catch: technically valid but wrong for right now

Why: That second class of problem stays a human decision, revisited deliberately.

items.prompt: What is the practical ceiling of a config-validation layer, as described in L3?
choices: It catches shape and presence bugs (missing, malformed, absurd values) but cannot judge whether a technically-valid value is the operationally right choice for current conditions
It has no ceiling — a sufficiently detailed validator can guarantee full correctness
It can only ever check that a value is present, nothing about its shape
It replaces the need for any human review of config changes
items.explanation: Validation is bounded to what can be checked mechanically from the value alone — it can't reason about whether 2000 req/s is enough for an upcoming traffic spike, which requires human judgment informed by context validation doesn't have.
items.reference:
⚙️ validation catches: missing, malformed, absurd
🧠 validation can't catch: technically valid but wrong for right now

Why: That second class of problem stays a human decision, revisited deliberately.

items.prompt: A connection-pool size passes its own range check, but is still larger than the database's actual max-connections limit. Would a single-field range check on the pool size alone have caught this?
choices: No — this requires a cross-field check comparing two config values against each other, not a check on either value in isolation
Yes, any range check on a positive integer automatically accounts for other systems' limits
No, because pool size can never be validated at all
Yes, because the database's limit is always baked into the range bounds automatically
items.explanation: Each value can be individually well-formed and still be wrong together — catching this needs a rule that looks across multiple config values at once, extending the same validation pattern to compare fields against each other rather than each field against a fixed range.
items.reference:
⚙️ validation catches: missing, malformed, absurd
🧠 validation can't catch: technically valid but wrong for right now

Why: That second class of problem stays a human decision, revisited deliberately.

items.prompt: A feature flag needs to be turned off during an incident, without waiting for a redeploy. Does startup config validation alone solve this?
choices: No — startup validation only runs once, at boot; a runtime-toggleable flag needs its own mechanism that can change (and be validated) while the service is already running
Yes — startup validation automatically re-checks config continuously in the background
Yes, because feature flags are never allowed to change without a redeploy anyway
No, because feature flags can never be validated at all
items.explanation: Startup validation is, by definition, a one-time check at boot — a value that needs to change live requires a separate mechanism (a config service the app polls or subscribes to) with its own validation running continuously, not just once at startup.
items.reference:
🕒 startup validation: runs once, at boot
🔄 runtime-toggleable value: needs its own live mechanism + continuous validation

Why: Fail-fast still applies, it just can't be a one-time check anymore.

items.prompt: What has to change about the fail-fast validation approach for a config value that can be updated live, compared to one only read at startup?
choices: The validation logic itself can stay the same, but it needs to run every time the value changes, not just once at process boot
Validation is no longer needed at all for runtime-toggleable values
The value must be hardcoded into the application instead of being configurable
The application must be restarted every time the value changes, defeating the purpose of a runtime toggle
items.explanation: The fail-fast principle — check before accepting a bad value — still applies, but it has to run on every update to a live-toggleable value, not just once at startup, since the value can now change after the service is already serving traffic.
items.reference:
🕒 startup validation: runs once, at boot
🔄 runtime-toggleable value: needs its own live mechanism + continuous validation

Why: Fail-fast still applies, it just can't be a one-time check anymore.
